h1: Training bar staff to sell craft beer and raise average spend
title: Training Bar Staff to Sell Craft Beer | Craft Beer School
desc: How to train brewpub bar and floor staff to describe your beers, guide guests to the right one and raise average spend per cover without pushing drinking.
teaser: Your server is the last step in the brewing process. If they cannot describe the beer, the guest orders the one they already know.
standfirst: Most guests decide what to drink in the ten seconds after the server says hello. Here is how to train your team to use those seconds well, with tastings, simple language and incentives that reward good service rather than more pints.
sections:
A brewpub can brew six excellent beers and still sell mostly the lager, because the server could not explain the others. In India, where many guests are new to craft beer, the server is often the only guide they get. A confident two-line description turns a hesitant guest into one who tries something new and comes back for it.

The goal is a better visit, not more alcohol. Raising average spend per cover through flights, food pairings and takeaway is good for the guest and the business. Pushing extra rounds is neither.
Start with tasting, inside the rules

Staff cannot sell a beer they have never tasted. Run a short tasting before service when a new beer goes on tap, within your company policy and the law. Keep pours small, around 30 to 60 ml. Provide spit cups and water. Staff who do not drink alcohol can still learn the aroma, the colour and how guests describe it. They should never be pressured to taste.

Have the brewer lead it where possible. Five minutes on what went into the beer and what to look for teaches more than any printed sheet. Our guide on writing tasting notes that sell helps you turn the brewer's language into words guests understand.
Give every beer a simple script

Ask staff to learn three things per beer: what it is like in plain words, who might enjoy it and what it goes with. For example:

  • "A light, crisp lager, very easy drinking. Good if you usually drink a regular beer."
  • "A wheat beer with banana and clove notes from the yeast. Lovely with the chicken tikka."
  • "Our IPA. Bitter and piney, the strongest hop flavour on the menu. Try a taster first if you are not sure."

Avoid jargon at the table. "IBU" and "attenuation" mean nothing to most guests. "Bitter like grapefruit peel" does. The menu itself should do some of this work, which our guide on reading a taproom menu looks at from the guest's side.

Instead of asking "what would you like?", train staff to ask:

  1. What do you usually drink?
  2. Do you prefer something light and crisp, or something with more flavour?
  3. Would you like to try a small taster first?

Those answers point to the right beer almost every time. Where your licence permits it, a free taster of 30 ml costs little and removes the fear of ordering the wrong thing. A guest who likes the taster orders a full glass with confidence.

The best ways to raise spend per cover also make the visit better:

  • Flights. Four or five small pours let a table explore the menu. Our beer flight guide covers building and serving them.
  • Food pairings. A server who suggests the right starter with a beer sells both. Food also helps guests drink at a sensible pace.
  • Takeaway. Where the licence allows growlers or cans to go, a guest who loved a beer may take some home.
  • Merchandise. Glassware and t-shirts for the regulars who want them.
Responsible service is part of the training

Train every server to recognise when a guest has had enough and to slow or stop service politely. Never serve anyone under the legal drinking age in your state. Check ID when in doubt. Offer water with every round and make the non-alcoholic menu as easy to order as the beer. Make sure staff know they will be backed by management when they refuse service.

Role-play the hard moments in training: the regular who wants one more, the birthday table that is getting loud, the guest who insists on driving. A server who has practised the words once will use them calmly on a busy Saturday. One who has not will usually just pour.

Track average spend per cover and flights per table by shift, not litres per head. Recognise the servers who sell flights and pairings and who get good feedback. Retrain monthly, because staff turnover in hospitality is high and a new server needs the same induction the old one had. A floor detail that works: a laminated card at each station with the current taps, the three-line script for each and today's food pairing.
faqs: How do I train bar staff who do not drink?
They can learn each beer's aroma, colour, style and pairing without tasting. Never pressure anyone to taste; their descriptions can be just as good.
What is the best way to raise average spend in a brewpub?
Sell flights, food pairings and takeaway where your licence allows. Measure spend per cover rather than litres per head.
How often should staff training happen?
Run a short tasting and briefing whenever a new beer goes on tap and a refresher every month, so new staff catch up quickly.
